To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

teachers of vocational and non-vocal English classes are teaching character, that the curricula of these classes are not explicitly designed to teach character, and that the character that these teachers and their students are teaching is a version of the character of the Protestant work ethic.
the character curriculum for students in vocational and nonvocational classes is implicit and includes instruction in broad dispositions that support students' success in school and in life.
the curricula for working-class students that these teachers taught represented a range of explicit attention to character education.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how working class students and the teachers who teach them are socialized into a particular set of beliefs about what it means to be a working class student and what the role of the teacher is in that process.
the ways in which the social class of students is taken up by their teachers and their schools, and the implications of these social class assumptions and practices for the lives of students.
how teachers and schools are responding to the challenges of teaching students from working-class homes and the implications for the future of these students.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the teachers in this study taught character education to students who were presumed to lack character, and the character education they taught was designed for the students to be prepared to succeed in a world that is organized to benefit those who have character.

the curriculum of working class students is one that is implicitly and explicitly focused on the development of the students' character, and this focus on character is a means by which students are taught to engage in the work that is necessary to achieve success in the school system.
the character curriculum in vocational English classes is an implicit part.of the education for students of lower socioeconomic status.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

teachers and students are social actors in a social system that is not neutral, and that the system is designed to produce particular types of social futures for students from poor and lower class backgrounds, futures that include the possibility of working class jobs and a life of poverty, and that these futures are produced through the curriculum that is offered to these students, including the implicit curriculum of character education that is embedded in the curricula of vocational and non-vocal English classes.

teachers are expected to teach students from poor and low-income backgrounds the skills and traits necessary to be productive members of the workforce and the society, while students from middle- and upper-class backgrounds are expected to develop these traits and skills on their own through the implicit character curriculum of the school and the community.
character education is a form of cultural capital, and it is a form of social capital that is not equally accessible to all students.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the character of students from working class backgrounds is not assumed to be in need of improvement, as the character curriculum in their schools and classrooms is designed to improve their work ethic.

the teachers in our study were not aware of the extent to which they were engaging in character education, nor did they see themselves as having the power to make choices about the content of their curricula.

character education in schools is not a matter of whether or not to include character education in the curriculum, but rather, what character traits are included and how they are taught, and that these questions are not being asked with the same urgency in the vocational and nonvocational classes of working class and poor students as in other classes.
